hints: Look closely at the shape in the photo. You see lots of large, thin-walled, interconnected air spaces like a honeycomb, not a tube with a thick wall.
Think which part of the gas exchange system has this spongy look, and which very thin tissue must line it to keep the diffusion distance for oxygen as short as possible.
walkthrough:
**Observe what the photomicrograph shows**

Look at the structure first. You can see many open white spaces separated by very, very thin dark lines with tiny nuclei.

This is the classic spongy appearance of alveoli in the lungs, not a trachea or bronchus in cross section.

**Recall where each tissue is found**

Cartilage, ciliated epithelium with goblet cells, and smooth muscle are all found in the walls of the larger airways like the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to support them, move mucus and control diameter.

Alveoli do not need those tissues. They need walls that are one cell thick for rapid gas exchange.

**Link alveoli to squamous epithelium**

Alveoli are lined by squamous (flattened) epithelium. The cells are extremely thin and flat, which you see as the delicate walls in the photo.

This creates a short diffusion pathway: alveolar air to blood in the surrounding capillaries. So D is the tissue you can see.

options.A: Cartilage is a thick, solid supporting tissue found in trachea and bronchi, not the delicate thin walls of alveoli seen here.
options.B: Ciliated epithelium lines the larger airways to move mucus, but alveoli have no cilia and have much thinner walls than ciliated cells.
options.C: Smooth muscle is found in bronchiole walls to constrict airways, not in the thin single-celled walls of alveoli.
options.D: The thin walls of the alveoli are made of squamous epithelium, flattened cells ideal for short-distance diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
